title: Core programming concepts
description: Everyday software vocabulary that isn't the name of a specific package — the words vibe coders trip on that the package/library dictionary never covers.

component.definition: A reusable, self-contained chunk of UI — usually one file — that you compose together to build a screen.

props.definition: The inputs passed into a component from its parent, similar to arguments passed into a function.

state.definition: Data a component remembers between renders — when it changes, the component redraws itself on screen.

hook.definition: A function starting with `use` (like useState or useEffect) that lets a component tap into features such as state or lifecycle events.

render.definition: The process of turning component code into the actual HTML shown on screen.

DOM.definition: The browser's live, in-memory tree of every element on the page, which JavaScript can read and change.

virtual DOM.definition: A lightweight in-memory copy of the page a UI library compares against the real page to figure out the smallest possible update.

JSX.definition: A syntax that lets you write HTML-like markup directly inside JavaScript, which tools compile down to real function calls.

single-page app.definition: A web app that loads one HTML page once and then swaps content in and out with JavaScript, instead of requesting a whole new page for every click.

server-side rendering.definition: Generating a page's HTML on the server before sending it to the browser, instead of building it entirely with JavaScript after the page loads.

route.definition: A rule that matches a URL, like /about, to the specific screen, component, or handler that should respond to it.

routing.definition: The system that matches an incoming URL to the code that should handle it.

client-side routing.definition: Switching between screens by updating the URL and swapping components in the browser, without asking the server for a new page.

CSS.definition: The language that controls how HTML looks — colors, spacing, layout, fonts — kept separate from the content itself.

responsive design.definition: Building a layout that automatically rearranges itself to look right on any screen size, from a phone to a desktop.

design system.definition: A shared, reusable set of colors, fonts, spacing rules and components that keeps an app looking consistent.

animation.definition: Code that changes an element's appearance gradually over time, like fading something in or sliding it into view.

API.definition: A defined way for one piece of software to ask another piece of software to do something or hand back data.

REST API.definition: A common style of API where you ask for or change data by sending HTTP requests, like GET or POST, to specific URLs.

endpoint.definition: One specific URL an API exposes for a particular action, like /users or /login.

HTTP request.definition: A message a client, like a browser, sends to a server asking for something — a page, some data, or an action.

HTTP method.definition: The verb on an HTTP request that says what kind of action is being asked for — GET reads data, POST creates it, and so on.

middleware.definition: Code that runs between a request arriving and the final response being sent, often used for checking login status or logging.

database.definition: A system that stores data permanently on disk so it survives after the program that created it stops running.

ORM.definition: A library that lets you read and write database rows using regular code objects instead of writing raw SQL by hand.

migration.definition: A recorded, repeatable change to a database's structure, like adding a column, so every environment can apply it the same way.

CRUD.definition: The four basic things most apps do with data: Create, Read, Update, Delete.

schema.definition: The defined shape of a piece of data — what fields it has and what type each one is.

JSON.definition: A simple, widely-used text format for structured data — objects, lists, numbers, strings — that both humans and computers can read.

serialization.definition: Converting a data structure in memory into a format, like JSON, that can be saved or sent elsewhere.

cache.definition: Temporarily storing a result so the next request for the same thing can be answered instantly instead of redoing the work.

local storage.definition: A small key-value storage area inside the browser that a website can use to remember data between visits.

session.definition: A period of continuous activity the server recognizes as belonging to one logged-in user.

authentication.definition: Confirming that a user is who they say they are, usually by checking a password or a token.

authorization.definition: Deciding what an already-identified user is allowed to do or see.

token.definition: A piece of data, often a long random string, a server hands out to prove a user is logged in without re-sending a password on every request.

environment variable.definition: A named value set outside the code, like an API key or a database URL, that the program reads at runtime instead of hard-coding secrets.

CORS.definition: A browser security rule that blocks a webpage from calling an API on a different domain unless that API explicitly allows it.

webhook.definition: A URL your app exposes so another service can automatically notify it the instant something happens, instead of your app having to keep checking.

bundler.definition: A tool that takes many separate source files and combines them into the small number of files a browser actually loads.

build step.definition: The process of transforming source code — compiling, bundling, minifying — into the finished files that get deployed.

transpiler.definition: A tool that translates code written in one form, like modern JavaScript, into another form a browser or runtime can actually run.

compiler.definition: A tool that translates code from one language or form into another that a computer can run.

package manager.definition: A tool that downloads, installs, and tracks the external libraries a project depends on.

lockfile.definition: A file that pins the exact version of every dependency installed, so a project installs identically every time.

dependency.definition: An external library or package your code relies on to work.

dev dependency.definition: A package only needed while building or testing a project, not while it's actually running for users.

CLI.definition: A command-line interface — a tool you operate by typing text commands into a terminal, rather than clicking buttons.

hot reload.definition: A development feature that updates the running app in the browser the instant you save a file, without a full page refresh.

linter.definition: A tool that scans code for likely mistakes or style violations before you even run it.

linting.definition: The act of running a linter over code to catch likely mistakes or style violations before running it.

formatter.definition: A tool that automatically rewrites code into a consistent style — spacing, quotes, line length.

test runner.definition: A tool that finds and executes a project's test files and reports which ones passed or failed.

mock.definition: A fake stand-in for a real piece of code, like an API call, used in tests so the test doesn't depend on the real thing working.

deploy.definition: Publishing a new version of an app to the server or service where real users can reach it.

deployment.definition: The act of publishing a new version of an app so real users can reach it.

production.definition: The live version of an app that real users interact with, as opposed to a copy running on a developer's own machine.

serverless function.definition: A small piece of backend code that a cloud provider runs on demand for a single request, without you managing a server yourself.

CDN.definition: A network of servers spread around the world that serves static files, like images or scripts, from whichever copy is closest to the visitor.

static site.definition: A website made of pre-built HTML, CSS and JS files served as-is, with no server-side code generating pages on the fly.

environment.definition: One of the separate copies of an app's infrastructure — development, staging, production — used to test changes safely before real users see them.

repository.definition: A project's full set of files plus its entire tracked history, as managed by Git.

commit.definition: A saved snapshot of changes in Git, with a message describing what changed and why.

branch.definition: A separate line of development in Git, so changes can be made without touching the main version until ready to merge.

pull request.definition: A request to merge one branch's changes into another, usually reviewed by someone else before it's accepted.

CI/CD.definition: Automation that runs tests and deploys code automatically whenever changes are pushed, instead of doing it by hand.

function.definition: A named, reusable block of code that takes some input and, usually, returns a result.

class.definition: A blueprint for creating objects that bundle related data and behavior together.

async.definition: Code that can start a slow operation, like a network request, and keep running other things while it waits, instead of freezing until it finishes.

callback.definition: A function handed to another piece of code, to be called later once some operation finishes.

promise.definition: An object representing a value that isn't ready yet but will be, eventually — either successfully or with an error.

event listener.definition: Code that waits for something to happen, like a click or a key press, and runs in response.

namespace.definition: A named container that groups related names together so they don't clash with identically-named things elsewhere.

entry point.definition: The file or function where a program actually starts running.

framework.definition: A pre-built structure and set of rules for building an app, which you build within rather than starting from a blank file.

library.definition: A collection of pre-written code you can call into your own project to avoid writing it yourself.

HTML.definition: The markup language that defines the structure and content of a webpage — the text, images and elements a browser turns into a page.
